Confidence Interval for Eta Squared (Effect Size for ANOVA)

Source: R/ci_eta_squared.R
ci_eta_squared.Rd

Computes the point estimate of eta squared (\(\eta^2\)) of each effect of an analysis of variance and an exact, noncentrality-based confidence interval for its population value, for the partial and the total estimand (see eta_squared). With estimand = "all", the default, the function reports both; the interval from an effect's F statistic is an interval for the partial value, and the total has one only where it equals the partial value, in a one-way design (see Details). "total" or "partial" reports one estimand.

Usage

ci_eta_squared(
  object = NULL,
  estimand = c("all", "total", "partial"),
  F_value = NULL,
  df_effect = NULL,
  df_error = NULL,
  N = NULL,
  conf_level = 0.95,
  alpha_lower = NULL,
  alpha_upper = NULL
)

Arguments

object

Optional. A fitted model object of class aov, lm, or aovlist (multi-stratum aov fit, e.g.\ aov(y ~ A + Error(subject/A), data = d)). For multi-stratum fits the function walks every error stratum and returns one row per non-Residuals effect, identifying the stratum used. Give either object or the F interface, not both.

estimand

Which estimand to report: "all" (the default, both, with NA where the inputs determine no estimate or no interval), "total", or "partial". An estimand asked for by name for which the inputs determine no interval is refused (see Details).

F_value

Observed F-value, or a vector of the F statistics of several effects tested against the same error term.

df_effect

Numerator degrees of freedom for the effect (one value for each effect, or one for all).

df_error

Error (residual) degrees of freedom.

N

Total sample size, the total number of observations (derived automatically from a fitted model, via nobs(object) for single-stratum fits, or, for aovlist fits, recovered as one more than the sum of the effect and residual degrees of freedom across every stratum, which is the total number of observations). The confidence limits for the noncentrality parameter are converted into limits for \(\eta^2\) with N. For an F from a design with an Error() stratum, give the size of the effect's stratum instead (see Details): the number of subjects for an effect tested between subjects, and for an effect tested within subjects the stratum's total degrees of freedom, which is df_effect + df_error when the effect is the only one tested in its stratum, not the number of rows of the data. N must be at least df_effect + df_error.

conf_level

Desired confidence coverage; default 0.95. Used only when alpha_lower and alpha_upper are both NULL.

alpha_lower, alpha_upper

Optional Type I error on the lower and upper side. If both are NULL, a symmetric interval at conf_level is used. If both are supplied, conf_level is recomputed as 1 - alpha_lower - alpha_upper. The table records the coverage, 1 - alpha_lower - alpha_upper, as its level and, when the two tail areas differ, the areas themselves, which the line beneath the printed table, results_sentence, and the alpha_lower and alpha_upper columns of tidy() state; with a tail area of 0 the interval is a one-sided confidence bound.

Value

A data.frame (class dmar_ci_anova, printed through dmar_tbl) with one row per effect and the columns effect; for each estimand reported, its estimate and limits, eta_squared_total, eta_squared_total_ci_lower, eta_squared_total_ci_upper, eta_squared_partial, eta_squared_partial_ci_lower, and eta_squared_partial_ci_upper; stratum (for an aovlist fit); and F_value, df_effect, df_error, and N. With the F interface effect is "overall" (the names of F_value, when it has them, or effect_1, effect_2, and so on, for several). N is the number of observations (for the F interface, N as supplied). The limits of the F interface and of a single-stratum fit are converted with that N; the limits of an effect of an aovlist fit are converted with the size of its own stratum (see Details), so that its row's F, degrees of freedom, and that size, passed to the F interface, reproduce them. The size is not a column of the table: it is the sum of the Df column of the stratum's table in summary(object), plus one for the stratum that lies between subjects (id in Error(id / occasion)). The table records the confidence level of its intervals in its conf_level attribute (conf_level, or 1 - alpha_lower - alpha_upper when the tail areas are supplied), which the console prints beneath it and results_sentence reports; the estimand attribute records the estimand asked for, and the estimand_notes attribute names each estimate or interval that is NA with the reason, which the console also prints. tidy() gives one row per effect and estimand, with the limits in ci_lower and ci_upper (see dmar_tidiers).

Details

The function takes a fitted model (aov, lm, or an aovlist from aov() with an Error() term) or an F statistic with its degrees of freedom and N. For factorial and within-subjects designs it returns one row per effect, the partial value computed against that effect's own error stratum.

Point estimates. The partial value is \(\hat{\eta}^2_{\text{partial}} = df_{\text{effect}} F / (df_{\text{effect}} F + df_{\text{error}})\), which equals \(\mathit{SS}_{\text{effect}}/(\mathit{SS}_{\text{effect}} + \mathit{SS}_{\text{error}})\); the total value of a fitted model is \(\mathit{SS}_{\text{effect}}/\mathit{SS}_{\text{total}}\), with the corrected total sum of squares. They are the estimates of eta_squared, whose Details describe the two estimands and the sums of squares of a fitted model. An F statistic does not determine the total value, which the F interface reports as NA.

Confidence interval. The interval rests on the two principles Steiger (2004, pp. 167–168) sets out. A confidence interval for the noncentrality parameter \(\lambda\) of the effect's F test is found by inverting the noncentral F distribution (via ci_nc_F), and because \(\eta^2\) is an increasing function of \(\lambda\), the limits for \(\lambda\) map into limits for \(\eta^2\): $$\eta^2_{\text{bound}} = \frac{\lambda_{\text{bound}}}{\lambda_{\text{bound}} + N},$$ where N is the number of observations for an effect tested between subjects and the size of the effect's error stratum for an effect of an aovlist fit (see below). When the observed F is below the critical value that sets the lower limit, the lower limit for \(\lambda\), and so for \(\eta^2\), is 0. In a one-way design the interval is the one ci_pvaf and ci_omega_squared give, the population \(\eta^2\) and \(\omega^2\) being the same quantity; the functions differ there only in their point estimates.

What the interval estimates: the partial value. The population value of an effect's partial \(\eta^2\) is the value its sample counterpart converges to as the sample grows, which is how Steiger (2004, Eq. 35, p. 171) defines the population \(\rho^2\) of a one-way design. For an effect tested between subjects, in a one-way or a factorial design, \(\lambda = N \sigma^2_{\text{effect}} / \sigma^2_e\), with \(\sigma^2_{\text{effect}}\) the variance of the effect over all N observations and \(\sigma^2_e\) the within-cell variance, so the population partial \(\eta^2\), \(\sigma^2_{\text{effect}} / (\sigma^2_{\text{effect}} + \sigma^2_e)\), equals \(\lambda/(\lambda + N)\) at every sample size (Steiger, 2004, Eqs. 13, 15, 16, and 19, pp. 169–170, where it is written \(\omega^2\) and described as the proportion of the variance that remains after the other effects have been partialed out; Kelley, 2007, Eqs. 44, 45, and 50, p. 12). The interval converted with N is therefore exact for it, and each effect of a fitted aov or lm model is converted with the number of observations.

The total value. The population total \(\eta^2\) of an effect, \(\sigma^2_{\text{effect}}\) as a proportion of the variance due to every effect of the design and the error, depends on the noncentrality parameters of the other effects as well as on the effect's own, and the distribution of one F statistic carries no information about them. The intervals of Steiger (2004, pp. 169–171), Smithson (2003, pp. 43–44, where the correlation ratio of a factorial effect is “a squared partial correlation”), and Fidler and Thompson (2001, Table 8) for the effects of a fixed-effects factorial design are intervals for the partial value. In a one-way design the effect and the error are the whole design, the total and the partial value are the same quantity, and the interval of a fitted one-way model is reported for both. For an effect of a design with other effects, and for every effect of an aovlist fit (whose total includes the differences among subjects), no interval is formed for the total: with estimand = "all" its estimate is reported with NA limits, and estimand = "total" is refused with an error of class dmar_estimand_undetermined (see dmar_metadata). The F interface determines neither the total value nor its interval, since F does not say whether the design has other effects; for a one-way design give the fitted model, or use estimand = "partial", whose interval is then the total's too.

A conversion with the degrees of freedom. Smithson (2001, Eqs. 8 and 9, p. 618; 2003, Formulas 5.3 and 5.4, p. 43) defines the population \(\eta^2\) of a factorial effect in the same way, through the effect's variance over all N cases, but converts the limits with \(\lambda/(\lambda + u + v + 1)\), u and v being the effect and error degrees of freedom (2001, Eq. 11; 2003, Formula 5.6). That form comes from regression, where \(u + v + 1\) is the sample size (2001, Eq. 4, p. 612), and it agrees with his definition only when \(u + v + 1 = N\), as in a one-way design. For a factorial effect it is a convention for the conversion rather than a definition of the parameter: its limits are exact for \(\lambda/(\lambda + u + v + 1)\), a larger quantity that depends on the degrees of freedom of the design's other effects. For the 2 by 7 design with four observations per cell that both Steiger (2004, p. 171) and Smithson (2001, p. 619) analyze, the 90% limits for the interaction are [.008, .316] with N = 56 and [.009, .346] with 6 + 42 + 1 = 49, and those for the row effect are [.009, .234] with N = 56 and [.012, .280] with 1 + 42 + 1 = 44. Converted with 44, a 95% interval for that row effect covers the population value 94.5% of the time when the value is .02 and 91.9% of the time when it is .40. Fidler and Thompson (2001, Table 8, p. 596) computed their fixed-effects factorial intervals with Smithson's syntax, from the F values and their degrees of freedom alone. Supplying \(u + v + 1\) as N with estimand = "partial" reproduces such published limits.

Within-subjects designs. An effect of an aovlist fit is tested in its own error stratum, and the number of rows of the data is not a sample size for that test. Under compound symmetry, Steiger (2004, Eq. 58, p. 177) gives the noncentrality parameter of a one-way within-subjects design with n subjects and p occasions as \(\lambda = n \sum_j (\mu_j - \mu)^2 / [\sigma^2 (1 - \rho)]\). The sums of squares for the occasions and for their error grow as \(n \sum_j (\mu_j - \mu)^2\) and \(n (p - 1) \sigma^2 (1 - \rho)\), so the value the sample partial \(\eta^2\) converges to is \(\lambda/[\lambda + n(p - 1)]\), where \(n(p - 1)\) is the stratum's total degrees of freedom, \(df_{\text{effect}} + df_{\text{error}}\). Under sphericity the same holds for every effect of a within-subjects stratum, with the stratum's total degrees of freedom (those of its effects and its error) in place of \(n(p - 1)\), and each such effect is converted with that total. An effect in the between-subjects stratum of a mixed design is tested among the subjects' means, as an effect of a between-subjects design is tested among its observations, and is converted with the number of subjects, one more than that stratum's total degrees of freedom. Converted with the number of rows, \(np\), the interval of a within-subjects effect is for \(\lambda/(\lambda + np)\), a smaller quantity, which the sample partial \(\eta^2\) does not estimate. In the three-occasion analysis of pygmalion in vignette("DMAR", package = "DMAR"), F(2, 618) converted with the 930 rows gives the 95% interval [.111, .194], which lies below the estimate of .212; converted with 2 + 618 = 620, the interval is [.157, .265].

The literature cited here does not settle the within-subjects case. Steiger (2004, p. 176) restricts his procedures to completely between-subjects designs, noting that the noncentrality parameter of a repeated measures design confounds the effects of the treatments with the correlation among the observations (pp. 176–177), and the factorial examples of Smithson (2001, 2003) and Fidler and Thompson (2001) are between-subjects designs. The conversion of a within-subjects stratum given here follows from Steiger's Eq. 58 and rests, as the stratum's F test does, on sphericity. A within-subjects partial \(\eta^2\) also leaves the differences among subjects out of its denominator, so it is not comparable with a partial \(\eta^2\) from a between-subjects design (Bakeman, 2005, p. 380).

The F interface. The limits are converted with N as supplied. The function cannot tell a between-subjects factorial F, for which the total sample size properly exceeds \(df_{\text{effect}} + df_{\text{error}} + 1\), from a within-subjects F given with the number of rows, so it does not warn; for an F tested within subjects, supply the size of the effect's stratum as N.

Designs supported.

  • Between-subjects ANOVA: fitted aov/lm, or F, df, and N. Each effect's limits are converted with the number of observations.

  • Within-subjects or mixed ANOVA: fitted aovlist. Each effect's CI is built from its own stratum's F and residual df and converted with the size of that stratum: the number of subjects for the between-subjects stratum (the stratum of the outermost term of Error(), such as subject in Error(subject/time)) and the total degrees of freedom of a within-subjects stratum. The N column reports the total number of observations across all strata, and the stratum column identifies which error term each row used.

Sums of squares in factorial designs. When a fitted model is supplied, F-values are read from anova() (single-stratum) or summary() (multi-stratum), both of which use Type I (sequential) sums of squares in base R. For balanced designs Types I, II, and III agree; for unbalanced designs they differ. If Type II or III F-values are required, compute them with e.g.\ car::Anova(object, type = 3) and pass the relevant F, degrees of freedom, and N into the F interface. See the Details of eta_squared on the coding of factors that Type III tests depend on. factorial_anova applies sum-to-zero contrasts itself and reports partial \(\eta^2\) and partial \(\omega^2\) with their confidence intervals for between-subjects factorial designs.

References

Bakeman, R. (2005). Recommended effect size statistics for repeated measures designs. Behavior Research Methods, 37(3), 379–384. doi:10.3758/BF03192707

Bargmann, R. E. (1970). Interpretation and use of a generalized discriminant function. In R. C. Bose, I. M. Chakravarti, P. C. Mahalanobis, C. R. Rao, & K. J. C. Smith (Eds.), Essays in probability and statistics (pp. 35–60). University of North Carolina Press.

Fidler, F., & Thompson, B. (2001). Computing correct confidence intervals for ANOVA fixed- and random-effects effect sizes. Educational and Psychological Measurement, 61(4), 575–604. doi:10.1177/0013164401614003

Fleishman, A. I. (1980). Confidence intervals for correlation ratios. Educational and Psychological Measurement, 40(3), 659–670. doi:10.1177/001316448004000309

Kelley, K. (2007). Confidence intervals for standardized effect sizes: Theory, application, and implementation. Journal of Statistical Software, 20(8), 1–24. doi:10.18637/jss.v020.i08

Kelley, K., & Preacher, K. J. (2012). On effect size. Psychological Methods, 17, 137–152. doi:10.1037/a0028086

Maxwell, S. E., Delaney, H. D., & Kelley, K. (2027). Designing experiments and analyzing data: A model comparison perspective (4th ed.). Routledge. (See Chapter 3 on \(\eta^2\), Chapter 7 on factorial designs, and Chapter 11 on generalized \(\eta^2\) for within-subjects designs.)

Smithson, M. (2001). Correct confidence intervals for various regression effect sizes and parameters: The importance of noncentral distributions in computing intervals. Educational and Psychological Measurement, 61, 605–632. doi:10.1177/00131640121971392

Smithson, M. (2003). Confidence intervals. Thousand Oaks, CA: Sage Publications. doi:10.4135/9781412983761

Steiger, J. H. (2004). Beyond the F test: Effect size confidence intervals and tests of close fit in the analysis of variance and contrast analysis. Psychological Methods, 9(2), 164–182. doi:10.1037/1082-989X.9.2.164

Venables, W. (1975). Calculation of confidence intervals for noncentrality parameters. Journal of the Royal Statistical Society, Series B, 37(3), 406–412. doi:10.1111/j.2517-6161.1975.tb01554.x

Examples

# 1. The F interface. Bargmann's (1970) example, used in turn by
#    Venables (1975), Fleishman (1980), and Steiger (2004): a one-way
#    ANOVA with five groups of 11 and an observed F of 11.221 on 4 and
#    50 df, at 90%. F determines the partial value, which in a one-way
#    design is the total.
ci_eta_squared(F_value = 11.221, df_effect = 4, df_error = 50, N = 55,
               estimand = "partial", conf_level = 0.90)
#>  effect  eta_squared_partial eta_squared_partial_ci_lower
#>  overall 0.473               0.261                       
#>  eta_squared_partial_ci_upper F_value df_effect df_error N 
#>  0.565                        11.221  4         50       55
#> 
#> Confidence level: 90%

# 2. One-way ANOVA from a fitted model: mean IQ gain differs across
#    the six grades of the pygmalion data (N = 310). The total and the
#    partial value coincide, and so do their intervals.
fit_one <- aov(iq_gain ~ factor(grade), data = pygmalion)
ci_eta_squared(fit_one)
#>  effect        eta_squared_total eta_squared_total_ci_lower
#>  factor(grade) 0.118             0.048                     
#>  eta_squared_total_ci_upper eta_squared_partial eta_squared_partial_ci_lower
#>  0.176                      0.118               0.048                       
#>  eta_squared_partial_ci_upper F_value df_effect df_error N  
#>  0.176                        8.159   5         304      310
#> 
#> Confidence level: 95%

# 3. Two-factor ANOVA for the manipulated expectancy treatment and the
#    measured grade classification (pygmalion data, N = 310). The
#    treatment by grade interaction is weak here (F = 1.19), so the
#    additive model is used. The totals are reported without limits.
fit_additive <- aov(iq_8 ~ treatment + factor(grade), data = pygmalion)
ci_eta_squared(fit_additive)
#>  effect        eta_squared_total eta_squared_total_ci_lower
#>  treatment     0.020             <NA>                      
#>  factor(grade) 0.043             <NA>                      
#>  eta_squared_total_ci_upper eta_squared_partial eta_squared_partial_ci_lower
#>  <NA>                       0.021               0.001                       
#>  <NA>                       0.044               0.001                       
#>  eta_squared_partial_ci_upper F_value df_effect df_error N  
#>  0.062                        6.519   1         303      310
#>  0.082                        2.787   5         303      310
#> 
#> Confidence level: 95%
#> 
#> NA eta_squared_total limits: No confidence interval is formed for the total eta squared of an effect in a design with other effects or with an Error() term: the noncentral F interval from the effect's F is an interval for the partial value, and the total depends as well on the other effects of the design (see the Details of ?ci_eta_squared).

# 4. Within-subjects ANOVA. The partial value's interval is computed
#    against the within-subjects error stratum, named in 'stratum'.
set.seed(113)
n <- 20
rm_data <- data.frame(
  subject = factor(rep(seq_len(n), each = 3)),
  time    = factor(rep(c("Pre", "Mid", "Post"), n),
                   levels = c("Pre", "Mid", "Post")),
  y       = rnorm(n, sd = 1.5)[rep(seq_len(n), each = 3)] +
            0.7 * rep(1:3, n) + rnorm(n * 3, sd = 1.2)
)
fit_rm <- aov(y ~ time + Error(subject/time), data = rm_data)
ci_eta_squared(fit_rm, estimand = "partial")
#>  effect eta_squared_partial eta_squared_partial_ci_lower
#>  time   0.231               0.023                       
#>  eta_squared_partial_ci_upper stratum      F_value df_effect df_error N 
#>  0.417                        subject:time 5.701   2         38       60
#> 
#> Confidence level: 95%

# 5. The size with which the limits are converted. The interaction of
#    the 2 by 7 design with four observations per cell analyzed by
#    Steiger (2004, p. 171), F = 2.50 on 6 and 42 df, at 90%: the
#    total sample size of 56 gives the interval for the population
#    partial eta squared, and 6 + 42 + 1 = 49 gives the limits that
#    Smithson (2001) reports for the same F.
ci_eta_squared(F_value = 2.50, df_effect = 6, df_error = 42, N = 56,
               estimand = "partial", conf_level = 0.90)
#>  effect  eta_squared_partial eta_squared_partial_ci_lower
#>  overall 0.263               0.008                       
#>  eta_squared_partial_ci_upper F_value df_effect df_error N 
#>  0.316                        2.500   6         42       56
#> 
#> Confidence level: 90%
ci_eta_squared(F_value = 2.50, df_effect = 6, df_error = 42, N = 49,
               estimand = "partial", conf_level = 0.90)
#>  effect  eta_squared_partial eta_squared_partial_ci_lower
#>  overall 0.263               0.009                       
#>  eta_squared_partial_ci_upper F_value df_effect df_error N 
#>  0.346                        2.500   6         42       49
#> 
#> Confidence level: 90%

# 6. A within-subjects F from a report: the three IQ occasions of the
#    pygmalion data, F(2, 618) = 83.11 for 310 children. N is the
#    620 degrees of freedom of the occasion stratum, not 930 rows.
ci_eta_squared(F_value = 83.11, df_effect = 2, df_error = 618, N = 620,
               estimand = "partial")
#>  effect  eta_squared_partial eta_squared_partial_ci_lower
#>  overall 0.212               0.157                       
#>  eta_squared_partial_ci_upper F_value df_effect df_error N  
#>  0.265                        83.110  2         618      620
#> 
#> Confidence level: 95%
